# turbovec against FAISS on four CPU cores — the run

What was run on 2026-09-14, on this session's container, and what it
measured. The script is [`bench.py`](https://github.com/Collegica/collegica-code/tree/main/docs/research/2026-09-14-turbovec/notes/bench.py); the raw output is
[`results_t1.json`](https://github.com/Collegica/collegica-code/tree/main/docs/research/2026-09-14-turbovec/notes/results_t1.json) (one thread) and
[`results_t4.json`](https://github.com/Collegica/collegica-code/tree/main/docs/research/2026-09-14-turbovec/notes/results_t4.json) (four threads). Every number below is
copied from those files.

## The machine

Ubuntu 24.04 in a container, 4 vCPUs (Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, Sapphire
Rapids generation: AVX-512 with VNNI, VBMI and BF16), 15 GB of RAM, no
GPU. Python 3.12 in a `uv` virtual environment. Hugging Face was
unreachable; the datasets came from a public Google Cloud Storage mirror
of the ann-benchmarks HDF5 files.

## What was installed

`uv pip install turbovec faiss-cpu numpy h5py` on Python 3.12 — two
seconds, 126 MB.

| Package | Version | Uploaded |
|---|---|---|
| `turbovec` | 1.0.0 | 2026-08-18 |
| `faiss-cpu` | 1.15.0 | 2026-08-03 |
| `numpy` | 2.5.3 | |

## The datasets

| Set | Vectors used | Queries | Dimension | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GloVe-100 (`glove-100-angular.hdf5`) | 100,000 sampled from 1,183,514 (seed 42) | 1,000 | 100, zero-padded to 104 for turbovec | ann-benchmarks |
| DBpedia/OpenAI (`dbpedia-100k-openai-ada002-angular.hdf5`) | 100,000 | 973 (all the file has) | 1536 | ann-benchmarks "custom", `text-embedding-ada-002` |

Both are "angular" sets, so every vector and query was L2-normalised and
searched by inner product. Ground truth (exact top-10 per query) was
recomputed with `faiss.IndexFlatIP` over the 100,000 vectors actually
indexed, since the files' own neighbour lists refer to the full corpus.
turbovec requires `dim` to be a multiple of 8; GloVe's 100 was padded with
four zero columns, which changes no inner product and adds 4% to its code
bytes. The DBpedia file stores float64; turbovec refuses anything but
float32, so it was cast first.

## What was compared

Every method searches the same queries at k = 64. Search time is the
median of five passes over all queries, reported per query, with the
thread count pinned for both libraries (`RAYON_NUM_THREADS` for turbovec,
`faiss.omp_set_num_threads` for FAISS). Index size is `len(to_bytes())`
for turbovec and `faiss.serialize_index(...).nbytes` for FAISS, so both
include their headers.

- **Exact**: `IndexFlatIP`, float32 — the reference.
- **turbovec** at 2, 3 and 4 bits, uncalibrated ("TQ") and calibrated
  ("TQ+", `calibrate()` on 1,024 random rows before `add()`), `prepare()`
  called so the first search pays no one-time cost.
- **FAISS PQ** (`IndexPQ`, nbits = 8, 256-entry codebooks) with m = d/2
  (4 bits per dimension, the turbovec 4-bit rate) and m = d/4 (2 bits per
  dimension) — the recall baseline turbovec's own suite uses.
- **FAISS FastScan** (`IndexPQFastScan`, nbits = 4) with m = d (4-bit
  rate) and m = d/2 (2-bit rate) — the speed baseline turbovec's suite
  uses.
- **FAISS scalar quantization** (`IndexScalarQuantizer`) at 8 and 4 bits —
  what "just round the coordinates" without a rotation gives.
- **FAISS HNSW** (`IndexHNSWFlat`, M = 32, efSearch = 128) over float32 —
  the graph alternative, for context.

Recall is measured three ways. **R@1@k**: how often the true top-1 is in
the returned top k (k = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64; the JSON has all of them).
**R@10@10**: the share of the true top-10 present in the returned top-10.
**Rerank**: for every quantized method, the returned top-64 rescored
exactly against the float32 vectors, then R@1@1 and R@10@10 again.

Finally the **allowlist** test: 1,000 of the 100,000 ids allowed (1%),
exact ground truth recomputed over the allowed set only; `IdMapIndex`
4-bit with `search(..., allowlist=)` against fetching the unfiltered
top-1,000 from the same index and dropping the disallowed ids.

## Results, four threads

Sizes and recalls are identical to the one-thread run (same seeds, same
codes); only the times change.

| Method | DBpedia ms/query, 1 → 4 threads | Speed-up | GloVe ms/query, 1 → 4 | Speed-up |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| exact float32 | 7.620 → 2.127 | 3.6× | 1.508 → 0.465 | 3.2× |
| TQ+ 2-bit | 0.983 → 0.242 | 4.1× | 0.184 → 0.058 | 3.2× |
| TQ 4-bit | 0.770 → 0.206 | 3.7× | 0.128 → 0.048 | 2.7× |
| TQ+ 4-bit | 0.791 → 0.204 | 3.9× | 0.139 → 0.046 | 3.0× |
| PQ8, 4-bit rate | 33.490 → 8.507 | 3.9× | 1.387 → 0.352 | 3.9× |
| FastScan, 4-bit rate | 2.089 → 0.554 | 3.8× | 0.147 → 0.050 | 2.9× |
| FastScan, 2-bit rate | 0.974 → 0.260 | 3.7× | 0.095 → 0.028 | 3.4× |
| SQ 8-bit | 17.089 → 4.434 | 3.9× | 9.290 → 2.576 | 3.6× |
| HNSW32 float32 | 1.052 → 0.244 | 4.3× | 0.253 → 0.065 | 3.9× |

Allowlist at four threads: DBpedia 0.070 ms (post-filter 1.494 ms); GloVe
0.013 ms (post-filter 1.304 ms). Build times at four threads: turbovec
0.8–2.3 s on DBpedia, PQ8 40–68 s, FastScan 5–13 s, HNSW 11 s.

Everything scales by three to four on four cores and the ratios between
methods hold: on DBpedia, turbovec 4-bit stays 2.7× faster than FastScan at
the same bit rate (0.204 against 0.554 ms) and level with it at 2 bits
(0.242 against 0.260); on GloVe, FastScan stays about twice as fast at the
2-bit rate (0.028 against 0.058) and level at 4 bits (0.050 against 0.046).

## Reading the numbers

- **Compression.** DBpedia: 614.4 MB → 39.6 MB at 2 bits (15.5×) and
  78.8 MB at 4 bits (7.8×). GloVe: 40.0 → 3.1 (12.9×, the padding to 104
  costing a little) and 5.7 (7.0×). The README's own `compression.json`
  says 15.8× and 8.0× at d = 1536; the difference is header and per-vector
  scales at this corpus size.
- **3 bits costs what 4 does.** TQ 3-bit is 78.8 MB — byte-identical in
  size to 4-bit — because "a byte holds only two codes" at 3 bits (API
  doc); it was also the slowest turbovec configuration and less accurate
  than 4-bit. Nothing recommends it in 1.0.
- **Recall at equal bytes, d = 1536.** TQ+ 4-bit 0.970 against PQ8 0.936
  and FastScan 0.855 at R@1@1; TQ+ 2-bit 0.817 against PQ8 0.780 and
  FastScan 0.756. At R@10@10 the same order: 0.963 / 0.941 / 0.880 and
  0.869 / 0.829 / 0.806. SQ8 at twice the bytes reaches 0.987.
- **Recall at equal bytes, d = 100.** TQ+ 4-bit 0.843 against PQ8 0.791
  and FastScan 0.741; TQ+ 2-bit 0.524 against 0.462 and 0.439. turbovec
  still leads, but 2 bits on 100 dimensions is a coin flip for everyone.
- **Calibration.** TQ+ over TQ: +2.8 points of R@1@1 at 4 bits and +1.8 at
  2 bits on DBpedia; +0.7 and +5.7 on GloVe; free in time.
- **Rerank.** With the top-64 rescored exactly, every quantized method
  reaches R@10@10 = 1.000 on DBpedia. On GloVe the 4-bit indexes reach
  0.998–1.000 and the 2-bit ones 0.920–0.960, turbovec ahead.
- **Search speed at equal bytes, d = 1536, one thread.** TQ 4-bit 0.770 ms
  against FastScan 2.089 (2.7×) and PQ8 33.490 (43×); TQ 2-bit 0.941
  against FastScan 0.974 (level) and PQ8 16.066 (17×). The exact scan is
  7.620 ms; HNSW over float32 1.052 ms at eight times the memory.
- **Search speed at d = 100.** TQ 4-bit 0.128 ms against FastScan 0.147
  (1.15×); TQ 2-bit 0.173–0.184 against FastScan 0.095 — FastScan is 1.9×
  faster at the 2-bit rate on low-dimensional data.
- **Build.** turbovec encodes 100,000 × 1536 in 2.7–2.9 s at one thread
  (about 28 µs per vector) with no training. FAISS PQ8 spent 52.7–87.7 s
  training codebooks, FastScan 8.6–18.3 s, HNSW 42.5 s.
- **Allowlist.** Filtering in the kernel: better recall (0.950 against
  0.865 on DBpedia; 0.899 against 0.834 on GloVe) and 20–110× less time
  than over-fetching 1,000 and post-filtering, because blocks with no
  allowed vectors are skipped.
- **HNSW's miss is a different kind.** Its R@1@1 equals its R@1@8 (0.944):
  when the graph fails to reach the true neighbour, asking for more
  results does not help. Quantizers misrank instead, and a rerank fixes
  misranking.

## What did not run

- Anything at the README's 10-million scale, or any corpus larger than
  100,000; the "faster than FAISS" comparison is verified at this size
  only.
- ARM. The README's Axion numbers are the author's.
- RaBitQ's own library (C++), the Elastic and Qdrant implementations, or
  the TurboQuant authors' code — this run compares turbovec with FAISS,
  not TurboQuant with RaBitQ.
- The framework drop-ins, `sync()` under crashes, and concurrent
  mutation.
- Any GPU.

## Traps

1. **`dim` must be a multiple of 8** — pad with zero columns; inner
   products are unchanged.
2. **float32 only** — the HDF5's float64 is refused, not converted.
3. **The log was empty for twenty minutes.** `python bench.py | grep -v
   warn | tee log` block-buffers `grep`'s output; the JSON file was the
   real signal. Use `--line-buffered` or write the log from Python.
4. **Single-threaded FAISS PQ training dominates the wall clock**: k-means
   for 768 sub-quantizers on 100,000 × 1536 took 88 s, HNSW 43 s; the whole
   one-thread pass ran about twenty minutes, the four-thread pass eight.
5. **Free the disk first.** The previous articles' environments (16 GB)
   had to be deleted before a 1.7 GB dataset would fit.
